items.title: ‘Totally Demonic’: Jonathan Cahn Reveals What Really Happened With the Viral Duct-Taped Man on Plane
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Celebrated author and Messianic rabbi Jonathan Cahn is making headlines after revealing that he was the unnamed passenger who drew the ire of an allegedly irate man who was so out of control he needed to be duct taped to an airplane seat.

Cahn shared his account of the disturbing incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618, proclaiming that the widely circulated images of a passenger being duct-taped — and media accounts of what unfolded — did not tell the full story.

He told CBN News he was returning home after a number of interviews promoting his new book, “The Altar of Pergamon,” when his assigned seat was unexpectedly changed shortly before the flight. Little did he know that his new placement on the plane would yield an experience he’d never forget.

Cahn ended up sitting beside a man who he said initially appeared friendly. In fact, the two talked for roughly two hours, with the passenger asking about his books and discussing his own family — but then the situation shifted after Cahn prayed about whether God wanted him to share his faith with the man.

“I said, ‘Give me an opening to share salvation with him, and share love with him,’” he said.

According to Cahn, the conversation turned toward faith, and he shared his testimony of once being an atheist and eventually coming to believe in God. Then, he said, the man’s behavior abruptly changed.

“At that moment, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he said. “His face changes. His voice changes.”

Cahn described the transformation as dramatic and spiritual, saying, “It was like someone getting taken over.”

He said the passenger began cursing Jesus and God, making vulgar statements and disturbing other people aboard the aircraft. Cahn said the man later became friendly again before allegedly putting his hands around Cahn’s neck and lightly striking him.

One of the most unusual moments involved Cahn’s laptop. At one point, a black line appeared on his screen. He said the passenger then reached over and tapped the computer, forcing the black area to spread across the entire screen.

Cahn said the computer was particularly important because it contained his writings and other projects.

Then, the author felt God tell him to protect his computer because the devil would use the man to destroy it. Listening to this warning, he attempted to leave his seat with the laptop and alleged that this is when the passenger lunged for it.

“We are wrestling on the plane,” Cahn said, noting that the computer became the focal point of the chaos. “I mean, we are literally wrestling.”

Cahn said the pilot contacted the ground for an emergency landing as the confrontation continued. Eventually, two passengers, including a retired police officer, intervened. Flight attendants provided duct tape to restrain the man, and the plane landed in Baltimore, where authorities took the man into custody.

The irony of the entire incident is that Cohn’s latest book “The Altar of Pergamon” — which came out just before this incident — deals with themes surrounding the devil and spiritual warfare. He believes some of what unfolded on the flight is rooted in that spiritual battle.

“The warfare is real, the enemy is real, and God is real,” he said.

Despite what happened, Cahn said he has no desire to condemn the passenger. Instead, he said he prays for him, and he even delivered a message to him.

“God loves you,” he said. “God’s arms are open. He loves you and He’ll receive you and wash that all away and give you a new beginning.”

Watch the full interview for more on this shocking story.

items.title: Southern Miss Football Coach Makes Bold Faith Declaration Ahead of Big Win
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Football season is just now getting underway, but Southern Miss head coach Blake Anderson drew a lot of attention before his players ever hit the gridiron Saturday.

Ahead of kickoff, Anderson wore a black long-sleeve shirt with the words “Christ Is King” emblazoned in yellow letters across the chest as he and the University of Southern Mississippi team performed took part in the “Eagle Walk” to the stadium.

The team went on to win an impressive 49-3 victory against Alcorn State University.

“I’ve had a bunch of people comment, and I’m pleased that it was noticed,” Anderson said during his weekly press conference. “I mean, the whole point of wearing it was for Christ to be glorified and it to be noticed.”

“I’m super grateful for my bosses that allowed me to be religious [and] use my platform to share my faith,” he continued. “[That is] not probably an easy decision for an AD and a president. But, you know, those are my views. That’s just me trying to use my platform.”

Anderson went on to say he is “saved by grace” and credited God with his success as a coach.

While bold public stances like his often garner criticism, the head football coach said he is thankful the responses online have been overwhelmingly positive.

“You never know what kind of response you’re going to get,” he admitted. “It’s been 99% positive and a few negative, which is what I expected. I wasn’t completely aware of just where it would go.”

He added, “In my opinion, if it makes one person think, then it was worth it.”

Anderson has been vocal about his faith for several years, even through incredible tragedies.

His wife, Wendy, died of breast cancer in 2019, followed soon after by the passing of his father. Anderson’s son, Cason, took his life in 2022, and the coach’s brother, Bryan, died in 2024, following a lengthy battle with aggressive colon cancer.

One of Anderson’s close friends, Larry Fedora, said he “wouldn’t have been able to survive if he didn’t have such a strong faith.”

In 2020, when he was the head coach of Utah State, Anderson told local reporters, “I’m a Christian before I’m anything else. I love the Lord and I feel like God put me in coaching.”

And in an interview five years later with Football Scoop, he said, “My faith comes from Christ, not from me. I’m not tough enough, I’m not big enough to do this on my own.”

items.title: boygenius’ Julien Baker Is Teasing Her First Solo Record in Five Years
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Julien Baker has been writing about God in public since she was 19. Prayer, doubt, addiction, grace and self-loathing — usually inside the same verse — and never once packaged as inspirational. She also hasn’t made a record on her own in five years. That looks like it’s about to change.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Julien Baker has been writing about God in public since she was 19. Prayer, doubt, addiction, grace and self-loathing — usually inside the same verse — and never once packaged as inspirational.

She also hasn’t made a record on her own in five years. That looks like it’s about to change.

This week Baker started leaving clues where people would find them.

She made a brand-new Instagram account, separate from the one she already has. It follows exactly three people. One is her. The other two are Calvin Lauber, who engineered her last record, and Matt Gilliam, who has played drums with her since they were kids in Memphis and was in her old band Forrister.

Gilliam is the interesting one. On 2021’s Little Oblivions, Baker played nearly everything herself — bass, drums, keys, banjo, mandolin. There are two videos on the account. Both show her walking into a practice space. Both cut off before she plays a note.

The newest post announces a last-minute set at the Blue Room inside Jack White’s Third Man Records in Nashville, with Kate Teague.

Five years is a long gap, though she hasn’t been idle. boygenius — Baker, Phoebe Bridgers and Lucy Dacus — released The Record in 2023, won three Grammys, played Saturday Night Live, and went on hiatus after a secret acoustic show in 2024.

Last April she and TORRES put out Send a Prayer My Way, a country album with both their names on it, then cut the tour short that May so Baker could focus on her health. She’s turned up on other people’s records since — Bridgers’ Lost Weekend, Turnstile’s covers collection. Last month she played a farm in Nantucket. In August she walked out during Dacus’ Outside Lands set to sing “Bullseye.”

Baker grew up in a Christian family in Memphis, left the Church, went back, and has been circling questions ever since.

“I never set out to be someone to speak about faith intentionally,” she told Denver’s Westword in 2016, when she was 20 with one record out. “I believe you can tell what is important to a person by what they talk about, and all my mental faculties are going to those questions about God. This is my experience, problems, concerns, how I feel — I’m never imposing a belief upon a listener.”

In the same conversation she named her reference points, and they’ll be familiar to anyone who spent their twenties in RELEVANT’s orbit: “I never wanted to make K-LOVE type music, but there are some artists that kind of toe the line, like Me Without You and Sufjan Stevens.”

She’s since said plainly which parts she kept.

“I don’t doubt God,” she told the New Statesman in 2021. “I am, in fact, certain that there’s something out there, even if it’s just God manifested in the dignity of other human beings.”

items.title: The Danger of Theologianology
items.author: Jack F. Trent
items.summary:
Jack F. Trent

Our happiness consists in knowing and loving reality, not what others have said about reality.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Jack F. Trent

The first question of St. Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae states that sacra doctrina—sacred teaching—is about God. Aquinas needs to make this point because the scientific status of sacra doctrina depends on the existence of an object that unifies the science. If physics is one by virtue of what it is about—mobile being—then sacra doctrina must be one by virtue of what it is about: God. What exactly Aquinas means by sacra doctrina is debated, but at the very least, theology is related to it. Aquinas is therefore committed to the proposition that theology is about God. 

So far, so uncontroversial. The very etymology of theology reveals its God-centered nature: theo + logia can be translated to “words about God.” Where is the profundity in Aquinas’s claim? The profundity lies here: Theology’s God-centered nature can be subtly replaced by a theologian-centered nature. Instead of studying God (i.e., doing theology), we may become content to merely study theologians (i.e., doing theologianology). This subtle change is a tragic problem. Whatever merit there is to studying theologians, it is not what will ultimately make us happy, flourishing human persons. 

Reality, Theology, and Theologians

Reality—that which is—can be known by the human person. Our faith teaches us this (see Rom 1:20) and so does human reason: Any attempt to deny the knowability of reality will presuppose some knowledge of reality, resulting in a contradiction. 

Our happiness depends on our ability to know and love reality. Only a real meal, a real spouse, or a real job can satisfy our desires. Simulacra fail to do the trick in the final analysis. Reality, however, comes in gradations. There simply is more being to a human person than a piece of meat. This truth is why a real spouse is more satisfying to possess than a real hamburger. It follows that the most satisfying of all reality will be that which possesses the most being: God. God, as Aquinas teaches, not only causes all being but is himself pure subsistent being, ipsum esse subsistens. To know and to love God are therefore the greatest and most satisfying activities human beings can undertake. 

We come to know God in this life first and foremost by means of Sacred Scripture and sacred tradition. Posteriorly, it is the task of theology to proceed from revealed principles and deepen our knowledge of God, his creation, and his redemption. Theology is faith seeking understanding, fides quarens intellectum.

Throughout the centuries God has blessed the Church by raising up illustrious theologians. Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and Pope John Paul II all readily come to mind. These theologians knew God in a profound way and shared their knowledge with the Church and the world by writing extensive and impressive works. Still, these works of theology, qua works of men and women, should never become the ultimate object of our study. That would be to commit ourselves to theologianology. 

Theologianology and Fr. Cajetan Cuddy, O.P.

In our day, the chief forewarner of the dangers of theologianology is Fr. Cajetan Cuddy, a Dominican priest of the province of St. Joseph, author, and assistant professor of Moral and Dogmatic Theology at the Dominican House of Studies. Fr. Cuddy has articulated the perils of theologianology at various conferences and on podcasts. His critique is captured by his analogy of the theologian and the astronomer. 

The true theologian is like an astronomer. As a master astronomer calibrates his telescope to achieve the best view of the stars, so does the master theologian calibrate his mind to achieve the best cognition of God. And as we might learn from the master astronomer, in order to calibrate our own telescope, so too might we learn from the master theologian in order to calibrate our own minds. 

The theologianologist is a different story. The theologianologist is like the astronomer who, instead of learning from the master and pointing his telescope into the night sky, points his telescope at the master astronomer. He obsesses over the master’s instruments, customs, and appearance, but sadly never gazes upon the beauty of the stars for himself. Such a sorry confusion mirrors the essence of theologianology. The theologianologist pores over the texts, sources, and styles of theologians, but ultimately never raises his gaze to God himself, his creation, or his saving plan. For any given theological question, the theologianologist is most concerned with “who said what?”

(I note here the essential problem of theologianology can plague subjects like philosophy as well. I chose to focus on theology because it is the highest science in which things matter most. And “philosopherology” simply does not have a ring to it, does it?)
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Theologianology can turn into a game of compare and contrast: “Augustine and Balthazar on hell,” “Bonaventure and Aquinas on the angelic will,” or questions of hermeneutics: “The Franciscan influence on Dei Verbum,” “Examining the twentieth-century Christian philosophy debates through a Neo-Suarezian lens.” Works like these (the above mentioned are fictitious—at least I did not look them up) are important but must always remain subordinated to actually making true claims about God, the world, and the human person.

Not even the Holy Scriptures should become the ultimate object of our study. The Church teaches us this fact when she states that “the Christian faith is not a ‘religion of the book.’ Christianity is the religion of the ‘Word’ of God, a word which is ‘not a written and mute word, but the Word which is incarnate and living’” (CCC 108). 

Keep in mind, our happiness consists in knowing and loving reality, not what others have said about reality. The true end of theology is God himself. To be satisfied with anything less is a pusillanimous rejection of God’s gift. Even if, after careful study, we err in our assent to the truth, this error can become an occasion for repentance, rectification, and correction. Making a false truth claim is missing a shot, but theologianology is refusing to shoot. 

The recognition of the dangers of theologianology nevertheless leaves untouched the absolute importance of tradition, deference to authority, and historical study. We stand in grave need for the Church and her saints to teach us how to see God correctly. I myself appeal to the authority of Aquinas and Fr. Cuddy! But my appeal to authority is in the hope that the reader will walk away thinking “Theologianology is dangerous,” not “Jack Trent and Fr. Cuddy think theologianology is dangerous.”

It may be safer, in some sense, to talk, write, and publish solely about theologians than it is to talk, write, and publish about God, but we simply cannot afford such a trade-off. Caution in study is needed, but God does not want us to be timid skeptics. We will find ourselves sealed off from the Lord of all reality if we contracept our minds from assent to the truth.

items.title: Thursday, September 10, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel today is taken from Jesus’s Sermon on the Plain in Luke. It is one of the more puzzling texts in the New Testament.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
1 Corinthians 8:1b-7, 11-13

Now concerning food sacrificed to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. Anyone who claims to know something does not yet have the necessary knowledge;  but anyone who loves God is known by him.

Hence, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “no idol in the world really exists,” and that “there is no God but one.” Indeed, even though there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as in fact there are many gods and many lords— yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

It is not everyone, however, who has this knowledge. Since some have become so accustomed to idols until now, they still think of the food they eat as food offered to an idol; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.

So by your knowledge those weak believers for whom Christ died are destroyed. But when you thus sin against members of your family, and wound their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food is a cause of their falling, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause one of them to fall.

Psalm
Psalm 139:1b-3, 13-14ab, 23-24

  O Lord, you have searched me and known me.
You know when I sit down and when I rise up;
    you discern my thoughts from far away.
You search out my path and my lying down,
    and are acquainted with all my ways.
Search me, O God, and know my heart;
    test me and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me,
    and lead me in the way everlasting.

Gospel Reading
Luke 6:27-38

“But I say to you that listen, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also; and from anyone who takes away your coat do not withhold even your shirt. Give to everyone who begs from you; and if anyone takes away your goods, do not ask for them again. Do to others as you would have them do to you.

“If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive as much again. But love your enemies, do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. Your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind to the ungrateful and the wicked. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap; for the measure you give will be the measure you get back.”

Reflection

Friends, our Gospel today is taken from Jesus’s Sermon on the Plain in Luke. It is one of the more puzzling texts in the New Testament. It speaks of loving our enemies—not tolerating them or vaguely accepting them but loving them. When you hate your enemy, you confirm him as your enemy. But when you love him in response to his hatred, you confuse and confound him, taking away the very energy that feeds his hatred.

There is a form of oriental martial arts called aikido. The idea of aikido is to absorb the aggressive energy of your opponent, moving with it, continually frustrating him until he comes to the point of realizing that fighting is useless.

Some have pointed out that there is a great deal of this in Jesus’s strategy of nonviolence and love of the enemy. You creatively absorb the aggression of your opponent, really using it against him, to show him the futility of violence. So when someone insults you, send back a compliment instead of an insult.
